summary:
Mission Forge is a browser-based space mission design game, built as a single self-contained HTML file. The player picks one of three missions: Earth wildfire watching, Mars subsurface ice mapping, or Moon south-pole water hunting. Then they design a spacecraft step by step: body, power system, antenna, science instruments, orbit, and launch rocket.

A live dashboard tracks mass, power, budget, and data against limits, which must all stay in the green. On launch, a canvas animation plays and random events (solar storm, antenna glitch, micrometeoroid hit, or good luck) can change the outcome. A report then explains what worked and scores the mission out of 120 points across success, science, efficiency, and decisions.

It uses Three.js for the 3D spacecraft view and canvas for the starfield and launch animation. Real NASA data grounds it: Mars gets about 43% of Earth's sunlight, and orbit heights are realistic. Up to four players can team up with a shared code and split roles. Game numbers are simplified for learning, not actual NASA specifications.
details:
Mission Forge: Design, Launch, Learn

What it does and how it works
Mission Forge is a browser game where players design a space mission and then launch it. They choose a science goal: mapping subsurface ice on Mars, spotting wildfires from Earth orbit, or finding water in the Moon's shadowed south pole craters. Then they pick an orbit, spacecraft body, power system, antenna, instruments and launch vehicle.

A Design Workshop lets players build their own spacecraft by choosing body type, material, structure size, solar array, battery, dish, transmitter, radiators, propellant and heat shield. Every change rebuilds a live 3D model that can be rotated and zoomed, so shape, size and layout follow the player's engineering choices.

On launch, the simulation checks six things: rocket capacity, instrument payload, power, data sent to Earth, budget and the science goal. It plays an animated launch with a random space event, such as a solar storm, and gives a score out of 100 with a plain-language report.

If a launch fails, a built-in Mission Coach explains what went wrong in simple terms. It can apply fixes, explain how the game works, answer typed questions, show a working design and suggest next steps, like other missions or tighter budget challenges.

Benefits
Players learn real engineering trade-offs by trying them: more instruments need more power, more data capacity, more mass and more money. Failure is safe and useful, because each failed launch becomes a lesson. The game runs in any modern browser, on phones and laptops, with no installation or sign-up. There is no single right answer, so players can experiment and compare designs.

Intended impact
We want space mission design to feel understandable and fun for students and curious beginners. Players should finish a session knowing why real missions are built the way they are, and feeling that engineering is something they can try. The coach is meant to stop learners from giving up when a design does not work, turning frustration into curiosity about how NASA teams solve the same problems.

Tools and technology
We built Mission Forge with HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single self-contained file. three.js (WebGL) powers the interactive 3D spacecraft, and the HTML canvas draws the launch animation. Mission values draw on NASA public data, including fact sheets comparing sunlight at Mars and Earth, and real examples such as NASA's Mars radar ice findings, the LCROSS Moon water detection and the FIRMS wildfire system. Sources are listed inside the game. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write and debug code, including the coach and the workshop-to-3D connection. The game is hosted on GitHub Pages and needs only a device with a web browser.

How it is creative
Many space games focus on flying a ship. Mission Forge focuses on designing a mission and balancing limits. The spacecraft's appearance is generated directly from engineering choices, so the model is the design. The Mission Coach gives guidance exactly when players are stuck, and missions connect to real NASA science questions.

Factors our team considered
Accuracy versus simplicity: formulas are simplified but follow real relationships between power, mass, data, heat and cost. Accessibility: plain language, a mobile-friendly layout and no sign-up. Learning through failure: reports explain why something failed and what to try next. Replayability: many valid designs, random events and optional challenges. Openness: a single file with no server and cited public data. Limits: live team play works only inside Claude's platform, and the coach follows fixed rules rather than a live AI.
